review.note: Reply restricts objection to determinate Necessary; به عين حقيقته remains a syntactic crux.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: The author replies that this counter-objection applies only to someone who makes the necessary nature a determinate thing standing over against the other determinate things. It would then differ from external existence and be that to which existence necessarily belongs. If the commonality is one of meaning, and that nature is itself a case of external being, the unrestricted being predicated both of it and of other things must nevertheless differ from it and necessarily accompany it. The objection does not apply when we identify the Necessary with unrestricted, all-encompassing, self-subsistent existence. Nothing other than it sustains it, and it is distinguished from everything else by its own reality: everything other than it is sheer nonbeing, so it needs no extrinsic differentiator.

englishSentences.text: I say: this is a general counter-objection to the argument just given.

Its formulation is that, if all the premises of your argument showing that what is necessary through itself cannot be the nature to which unrestricted existence necessarily belongs were sound, unrestricted existence itself would likewise fail to be necessary, since the same argument applies to it.
The explanation is as follows.
The Necessary cannot be unrestricted existence itself.

For, if its reality admits intellectual instances, one instance must exist and the remaining instances must be impossible: it is impossible both that the necessary reality should have many actual instances and that none of them should exist.
Once it is established that only one instance exists while the others are impossible, that instance must exist through another, and so its necessity must be through another.
Likewise, the impossibility of the remaining instances must be through another, not through themselves.
The reason is that the necessary nature must be a specific nature;
otherwise its instances would have different realities, entailing composition in the Necessary, which is impossible.
If it is a specific nature, what its instances intrinsically require cannot differ.
Thus, if some instances required necessity and others impossibility [the reported alternative reading], that requirement would not arise through themselves but through another.
The Necessary would then depend on another for its necessity, which is plainly impossible.

If, instead, it cannot have intellectual instances for any of the four reasons previously mentioned, then either this unrestricted reality differs from the reality of particular external existences called possible existences, or it does not.

If it differs, the term existence is applied to it and to possible existences equivocally, not with a common meaning: the meanings are different, and all that they share is the application of the word.

If it does not differ from external existences, possible existences must be qualified by intrinsic necessity, since each particular instance of a reality must possess that reality's necessary concomitants.
The author replies that this counter-objection applies only to someone who makes the necessary nature a determinate thing standing over against the other determinate things.
It would then differ from external existence and be that to which existence necessarily belongs.

If the commonality is one of meaning, and that nature is itself a case of external being, the unrestricted being predicated both of it and of other things must nevertheless differ from it and necessarily accompany it.
The objection does not apply when we identify the Necessary with unrestricted, all-encompassing, self-subsistent existence.
Nothing other than it sustains it, and it is distinguished from everything else by its own reality: everything other than it is sheer nonbeing, so it needs no extrinsic differentiator.

In sum, once they hold that the Necessary is a particular determinate nature like the other determinate things, it follows that it differs from the unrestricted meaning predicated both of it and of what stands opposite it.
It must also stand opposite the other possible determinate things.
The consequences already stated then follow.

But if the Necessary is all-encompassing unrestricted existence, from which no relation, attribute, or instance—whether similar or incompatible—falls outside, none of the impossibilities facing those who assert such a determination applies.

One may object that this account must still entail one of two things: either there can be no possibility, possible things, or other quiddities, or there must be an aspect of possibility within the Necessary.
Both are plainly impossible.
We reply that, if the denial of possibility means denying it without qualification, the alleged consequence is not conceded.
If it means denying possibility of existence insofar as it is existence, the consequence is conceded, but its impossibility is not.
As explained in the prolegomenon, possibility is a consideration that attaches to things in respect of the manifestation of knowledge;
and the manifestation of knowledge is plainly distinct from the manifestation of existence.
Know that, for discerning people of spiritual taste, discussions of this kind belong among the clearest self-evident matters.
For other learned persons, bound by the necklaces of uncritical adherence, they are scarcely intelligible.
Nor is this surprising: ‘For anyone to whom God gives no light, there is no light.’

englishSentences.text: I say: the author now begins to state and answer objections to the apparent meaning of the doctrine of the people of realization.

These objections mislead disputants of weak understanding and shallow thought, and unsettle some seekers of guidance whose minds have grown accustomed to intellectual sophistries and dialectical associations.
One objection is this.

The unrestricted nature which they identify as the Necessary is considered without any conditions or relations whatever—even without this negative consideration itself, since, on their doctrine, it is not restricted by unrestrictedness.
If this nature were necessary through itself, the supposition would therefore be contradicted.
For, if it were necessary through itself and necessity were required by its essence, necessity could not be separated from it.
It would then no longer be unrestricted but would be qualified by intrinsic necessity.
A qualification means nothing other than the consideration of a meaning additional to the nature itself.
If that meaning is intrinsically required and necessarily accompanies it, it must be considered along with it.
Thus the unrestricted nature would not be unrestricted: a contradiction.
The author answers that the unrestricted nature, precisely as unrestricted, can possess necessary judgments which do not take it outside unrestrictedness.
Judgments do so only if they are additional to it through an additional extramental meaning, and their realization and attachment depend upon that external meaning.

But suppose they are intellectual considerations belonging to the nature in relation to itself, without any additional meaning contaminating its pure unrestrictedness and without an external relation ascribing restriction to it.
None of them then removes it from its extramental unrestrictedness or makes it externally qualified by any of them.

It should not be objected that every concept distinct from the unrestricted nature must, when considered along with it, take it outside intrinsic unrestrictedness—whether the concept is an intellectual consideration belonging to it through itself or an actual feature accruing to it from another.

We reply that this would follow only if these were additional extramental things joined to it, or if the source and origin of their attachment were something other than its intrinsic unrestrictedness.
When they are considerations arising in intellect precisely in view of that unrestrictedness, they do not remove it from it.
A thing cannot be incompatible with the very source from which it arises.
From this one can understand the basis of the distinction between divine names and cosmic names.

arabicClauses.text: أقول : هذا إشارة إلى ايرادين صعبين قد استشكلهما المستبصرون من اهل النظر غاية الاستشكال عند اكثر الأزكياء من المخالفين هما الدَّاء العضال ،
و الحقُّ ان كلًا منهما عِرق ،
يتشعّب منه فنون الشغب و الجدال ،
و اصل يتفرع عليه أغصان الشبه و أفنان الأشكال ،
لا ينحسم مادتها الا باستعانة من الحدس القويم و فكر عن شوائب التعصُّب و التقليد سليم ،
اما الأول منهما فمبنىٌّ على مقدمة عَدُّوها من المسلَّمات ،
لشدَّة اشتباهها بها ،
و هي ان الطبيعة المطلقة من حيث انّها مطلقة عند من ذهب منهم إلى وجودها لا يمكن ان تكون قائمة بنفسها في الأعيان بدون انضمامها بشيء من القيود ،
فان وجود المطلق على تقدير وجوده في رأيهم انّما هو وجود المقيَّد لا غير .
إذا تقرَّر هذا ،
فنقول ،
لو صحَّ ان تكون الطبيعة المطلقة من حيث هي مطلقة التي هي بديهيَّة التصوُّر عند الجمهور قائمة بنفسها في الأعيان بدون انضمامها إلى شيء من المخصصات ،
و يصدق عليها الوجوب بالذات بالبرهان ،
على ما سبق تحقيقه آنفاً ،

لم يتوجَّه بوجه من الوجوه ان يورد هاهنا ما ذكر

من الاحتمال ،
لا منعاً و لا نقضاً .
اما المنع فلامتناع تطرُّقه إلى مقدمتي الدليل حينئذ ،
اما الاولى ،
فلانّها مبرهنة ،
و اما الثانية ،
فلانَّها بديهيَّة ،
و اما النقض ،
فلان تخلُّف الحكم من الدليل ،
انّما يتصور فيما لا يكون من افراد ما استدل عليه ،
و الطبيعة الملزومة لمّا كانت من افراد المطلق من حيث انّه مطلق ،
لا يصلح لأن تكون صورة للنقض .
و إذا كان الأمر على هذا الوجه ،
فلا يصحُّ للعارف بطرق التحصيل و انحائه ان يشرع في جواب أمثاله ،
إذ الشروع في جواب ما لا يرد على قانون البحث و أساليب المناظرة في قوة الخطاء ،
على ان التزام الجواب مع انّه عدول عن طريقة التوجيه لا يفيد فائدة سوى تطويل الكلام ،
و تكثير المقدمات ،
و تمكين المخالف من المنع و النقض ،
و تزييف البيان ،
و كلُّ ذلك محذور في قواعد الجدل و قوانين البرهان .
و اما الثاني من الايرادين ،
فتقريره ،
انّه لو صحَّ ان يكون الوجود المطلق من حيث انّه مطلق واجباً للزم ان لا يكون وصفاً مشتركاً ،
بين ساير افراد الوجود ،
و التالي باطل ،
اما اللازمة فظاهرة ،
و اما بطلان التالي ،
فلانا نعلم بالضرورة ،
انَّ كل واحد من افراد الوجودات الممكنة العينيَّة الخاصَّة هو من افراد الوجود العيني المطلق ،
كما انّا نعلم بالضرورة ان الوجود الواجب بالذات المنافى لكل واحد من الوجودات الخاصَّة منافاة احد القسمين للآخر ايضاً من جملة افراده .
ثمَّ ان هاتين الشبهتين لما فيهما من المقدمات المقبولة المألوفة لأكثر افهام الأزكياء سيَّما تلك المقدمة التي هي مبنى الشبهة و أساسها ،
يحتاج دفعها إلى نوع من الحدس ،
إذ به يتخلَّص الذكي اللبيب من ربقة الخطابيات المقبولة و الجدليّات المموِّهة و الساذجة ،

و بسنوحه ينحلُّ عقود التقليدات

و الاعتقادات الراسخة - الراسجة - لما فيه من الخلوص - الخلوِّ - عن شوائب التصرُّفات التعمليَّة الناشية من القوى الادراكيَّة العمليَّة - العلمية - عند اقتناص المطالب النظرية ،
و لما فيه من الرُّسوخ و الطمأنينة اللازمة للعطايا الوهبيَّة الامتنانيَّة ،
و كانت النسبة بين الفكر و الحدس في طريق النظر كالنسبة بين السلوك و الجذبة في غيره ،
فلهذا قال في الجواب : ان الزَّكىَّ الحادس ،
يعلم يقيناً ان الكون العيني الكائن بنفسه في الخارج ،
الذي وجود سائر الأشياء في الخارج انّما هو باشراق بارقة من بوارق نوره و ظهورها بتناثر لمعة من لوامع ظهوره ،
يمتنع ان يتكوَّن في الخارج بشيء من الكائنات التي انّما يتكوَّن فيه به ،
و بمقارنته .
ثمَّ انَّ وضوح هذه المقدمة في مبادى العقول لما بلغ مبلغاً لا يرتاب فيه من له ادنى تميُّز فضلًا عن السّابقين في مضمار غوامض العقليات و معالق اليقينيات ،
أراد ان ينبّه على مرامى سهام سهوهم و مواطى خطوات خطائهم ،
اعتذاراً منهم على وقوعهم في هذا الخطاء الفاحش و الغلط الظاهر ،
و من نفسه على الاشتغال بجوابهم و تمكينهم من المنع و النقض ،
بقوله : و لكنَّ الجمهور انّما يعتقدون انّ حكم مطلقه حكم ساير المطلقات .
و تقرير ذلك انّهم لما رأوا ،
ان لسائر المطلقات حكماً و هو ان وجوده في الخارج لا يتحقَّق الا بعد تخصُّصه بالفصول المقوِّمة و العوارض المشخَّصة ،
و بالجملة ،
انما ينضمُّ إليه الوجود الخارجي ،
و يتقوم به في ضمن افراده ،
حسبوا ،
ان الوجود نفسه ايضاً من هذا القبيل ،
فحكموا ان المطلق منه لا يكون قائماً بنفسه ،
فلا يصلح للواجبيَّة - و يجب ان يكون له مخصِّص و مقوِّم ،
حتى يتقوَّم في الخارج و يصلح للواجبيَّة - و مثل قياسهم هذا في المشاهدات ،
كمثل من زعم في المبصرات من المحسوسات ،
انه لها لم يمكن ادراك شيء منها بدون ان يظهرها نور من الأنوار ،
و ذلك الاظهار ،
انّما يتمُّ بعد ان يكون لذلك المحسوس سطوح متلوِّنة ،
فكذلك النُّور ايضاً لأنّه من المبصرات يجب ان يكون ظهوره بنور آخر بشرائطه ،
الا ان الوهم لمّا كان ليس له دخل في المشاهدات ،
لم يقع شكٌّ للمشاهدين في المثال المحسوس ،
حتى لو أورد هذه الشبهة على الأعمى ،
لم يبعد ان يعجز عن الجواب بخلاف المسألة المبحوث عنها ،
فانّها لمّا كانت من المعاني العقليَّة ،
كان الأمر فيه بالنسبة إلى اكثر العقول العديمة البصيرة الواقعة تحت حكمى الوهم و الخيال ،
كما وقع للأعمى ،
فيما أورد عليه من المثال ،
و هذا من جملة حكم اللَّه البديعة ،
ان جعل الوهم حارساً لحضرته المنيعة ان يكون شريعة لكل بصيرة حولاء و فطانة بتراء ،

الا لعباده المخلصين الذين فتح اللَّه بصيرتهم بنور اليقين حتى رأوا الحق على ما هو عليه بنوره المبين « وَ مَنْ لَمْ يَجْعَلِ اللَّهُ لَهُ نُوراً فَما لَهُ مِنْ نُورٍ » اللهم اجعلنا ممن ليس للشيطان عليهم سلطان هذا كلام وقع في البين ،
فلا بُدَّ ان نرجع لما نحن بصدده ،
و نقول : انّهم لمّا لم يفرِّقوا بين المطلق هذا ،
و غيره من المطلقات ،
حتى اعتقدوا ،
ان حكم مطلق الوجود في عدم تحقُّقه الا في ضمن المقيَّد ،

حكم ساير المطلقات من الماهيّات

الحقيقيَّة العينيَّة المبهمة في نفسها المتحقِّقة بغيرها ،
لا يبعد ان يبادر إلى أذهانهم الاحتمال المذكور ،
و هو ان الواجب يجب ان يكون من الوجودات الخاصَّة و التعيُّنات الجزئيَّة ،
و الا يلزم ان يكون الواجب ممّا لا يقوم بنفسه في الخارج بل يحتاج في تحقُّقه و قيامه في الخارج إلى غيره ،
و حينئذ كان إبطال هذا الاحتمال بعد تسليم كون الإيراد مُوَجَّهاً على سبيل التنزُّل لا يكون خارجاً عن قانون التوجيه ،
بل دفع ساير الشبه المانعة لحصول اليقين و القطع العقلي في المحل الغير المألوف بالقياس إلى طباع الجمهور ،
و انّما يكون مفيداً بالنسبة إلى من اختصَّ منهم بفضل الذكاء فيكون التزامه في نظر التعليم واجباً ،
و ذلك ان جمهور اهل العقل من المناظرين انّما يعتكفون عند المسلَّمات و النظريّات الغير المحتاجة إلى شيء غير ترتيب الضروريات و الاوليّات ،
و اما امثال هذه المقدمات المحتاجة مع ذلك الترتيب الفكرى إلى ضرب من الحدس و الذَّوق يكون في غاية البعد عن طباعهم ،
فلا بدَّ من رفع الشبه المانعة لعروجهم إلى مراقى الحقائق ،
و ذلك و ان لم يكن مفيداً بالنسبة إلى كلّهم ،
لكن يكون مفيداً بالنسبة إلى من هو اشدُّ ذكاءً منهم و أبعد عن رذيلتى البلادة و رسوخ التقليد الوهمي و الخيالى .
و هذا تلويح بان الكلام في هذه الرسالة ليس مع الجمهور من اهل العقل ،
بل مع من اختص منهم بمزيد الذكاء و فضل التفطُّن ،
و مع هذا كلّه يكون له حدس قوى و كشف ذوقى .
ثمَّ لو سُلِّم ،
انّ دفع هذا الاحتمال لا توجيه له بالنسبة إلى المخالفين من الناظرين ،
لكن من البَيِّن ،
انَّ دفع ساير الاحتمالات و الشبه الممكنة الورود بالنسبة إلى الطالبين و المسترشدين ،
يكون اعداداً لأذهانهم الضعيفة ،
ان يلوح لهم الحقّ ،

فيكون منعاً للحركات الفكريَّة المشوِّشة لهم عن الاضطرابات المستفادة من الوساوس العادية و التقليدات المنكرة

الراسخة في نفوسهم القابلة الطالبة .
و لا شكَّ ان التعرُّض لما يوجب تنظيف المحلّ عن العقائد التقليديَّة الراسخة ،
و ما يوجبه من الحركات المشوشة ،
المانعة الذي هو هاهنا بمنزلة رفع الموانع ،
المعبَّر عنه بالتخلية ،
واجب في نظر التعليم و التعلُّم ،
كما انَّ التعرُّض لما يوجب اعداد المحل من المقدمات اليقينيَّة التي هي للاستفاضة بمنزلة المقتضى المسمّى بالتحلية ،
واجب .
في هذا النظر .

englishSentences.text: I say: this points to two difficult objections which reflective investigators have found profoundly troublesome.
Most discerning opponents regard them as an incurable affliction.
In truth, each is a root from which varieties of contentious dispute branch out, a foundation supporting boughs of doubt and perplexity.
Their source cannot be cut off without the aid of sound intellectual intuition and thought free of the taint of partisanship and uncritical adherence.
The first objection rests upon a premise counted among the conceded truths because of its strong resemblance to them.

The premise is that an unrestricted nature, insofar as it is unrestricted, cannot, even for those who admit its existence, subsist by itself in external reality without being conjoined with some qualification.
On their view, the existence of what is unrestricted—assuming it exists—is nothing other than the existence of what is qualified.
With this understood, the objection runs as follows.

Suppose that the unrestricted nature as unrestricted, whose conception the generality regard as self-evident, could subsist independently in external things without any particularizing factor, and that its intrinsic necessity had been demonstratively established, as was just argued.
There would then be no legitimate way of raising the previously mentioned possibility, either by denying a premise or by presenting a counter-instance.
Denial could not affect either premise of the argument: the first has been demonstrated, and the second is self-evident.
Nor would a counter-instance be available.
Failure of the conclusion to follow despite the proof would have to occur in something outside the instances covered by the proposition established;
but the nature to which existence necessarily belongs is itself an instance of the unrestricted as unrestricted, and so cannot serve as such a counter-instance.
If that is so, anyone acquainted with the methods of acquiring knowledge should not embark on answering objections of this kind.
Answering what has no standing under the rules of inquiry and disputation is virtually an error.

Apart from departing from proper argumentative procedure, undertaking an answer adds nothing except lengthening the discussion, multiplying premises, and enabling an opponent to deny, counter, and impugn the exposition.
All these are to be avoided according to the rules of dialectic and demonstration.
The second objection is this.
If unrestricted existence as unrestricted were necessary, it could not be an attribute common to the other instances of existence.
But that consequent is false.
The implication is obvious;
the falsity of the consequent follows because we necessarily know every particular possible external existence to be an instance of unrestricted external existence.
We likewise necessarily know intrinsically necessary existence—which excludes each particular possible existence as one division excludes the other—to be among its instances.
Both objections contain premises accepted by, and familiar to, most acute minds, especially the premise forming the foundation of the first difficulty.
Removing them therefore requires a kind of intellectual intuition.
Through it the discerning thinker escapes the bonds of accepted rhetorical propositions and deceptive or unsophisticated dialectical arguments.
When it dawns, the knots of inherited convictions and deeply rooted beliefs are loosened.

Intuition is free from the interference of contrived operations arising from the cognitive faculties during the pursuit of theoretical conclusions, and possesses the firmness and assurance accompanying freely bestowed gifts.
In reflective inquiry, the relation of discursive thought to intuition is like the relation of spiritual wayfaring to attraction in the other path.

For this reason the author replies that an intelligent person endowed with intuition knows with certainty that external being, subsisting of itself outside the mind, cannot acquire its being through any of the things which themselves acquire external being only through it and through conjunction with it.
Those other things exist only through the shining of a flash of its light and become manifest through the scattering of a gleam of its manifestation.

This premise is so evident to the first principles of intellect that even someone with the slightest discernment should have no doubt about it, much less those who lead the field in subtle intellectual questions and the difficult matters of certainty.
The author therefore wished to identify where their errors had gone astray.
In doing so he explains both how they came to commit this conspicuous mistake and why he himself undertakes to answer them, thereby permitting their denials and counter-objections.

Hence his words, ‘But the generality believe that what holds of its unrestricted form holds of the other unrestricted natures.’

The explanation is that they observe a rule applying to the other unrestricted natures: these do not exist externally until they have been specified by constitutive differentiae and individuating accidents.
In short, extramental existence attaches to them and sustains them within their instances.
They assume that existence itself is another case of the same kind.
They therefore conclude that unrestricted existence cannot subsist by itself and so cannot be the Necessary;
it must possess a particularizing and sustaining factor before it can subsist externally and qualify as necessary.

An analogous mistake in sensible experience would be to reason that, since no visible thing can be seen without some light making it manifest, and since that manifestation requires the sensible thing to have coloured surfaces, light too—as something visible—must be manifested by another light under the same conditions.
But because estimation has no role in overriding direct observation in this example, those who see it have no doubt.
Presented to a blind person, however, the objection might well leave him unable to answer.

Our present question concerns intelligible meanings, and most intellects lacking insight, subject to estimation and imagination, are in the same position as the blind person confronted with that example.

Among God's marvellous acts of wisdom is His making estimation a guard over His inaccessible presence, preventing it from becoming a watering-place open to every cross-eyed insight and mutilated cleverness.

An exception is made for His sincere servants, whose inward sight He opens by the light of certainty so that they see the Real as He is through His illuminating light: ‘For anyone to whom God gives no light, there is no light.’ O God, make us among those over whom Satan has no authority.
This has been a parenthetical remark;
we must return to the present purpose.

Because they fail to distinguish this unrestricted reality from other unrestricted natures, they believe that unrestricted existence is realized only within something qualified, just as real external quiddities, indeterminate in themselves, are realized through another.

It is therefore unsurprising that the stated possibility immediately occurs to them: the Necessary must be one of the particular existences and individual determinations, or else it would not be self-subsistent but would depend on another for its realization and subsistence outside the mind.
Refuting this possibility, after granting for argument's sake that the objection is properly raised, is not outside sound argumentative procedure.
Rather, removing doubts that obstruct intellectual certainty in a matter unfamiliar to ordinary dispositions benefits those distinguished by exceptional intelligence;
addressing them is therefore obligatory from the standpoint of instruction.
Most rational disputants remain with conceded premises and theoretical propositions requiring nothing beyond the arrangement of necessary and primary truths.
Premises which, in addition to that discursive arrangement, need a measure of intuition and spiritual taste lie very far from their accustomed dispositions.
The doubts obstructing their ascent toward the realities must therefore be removed.
Although this does not benefit all of them, it benefits the more intelligent and those furthest from dullness and deeply rooted submission to estimation and imagination.

This intimates that the treatise does not address the generality of rational thinkers, but those endowed with exceptional intelligence and discernment, together with powerful intuition and experiential unveiling.

Even conceding that answering this possibility has no proper argumentative role with such opponents, removing the various objections and doubts that may occur to students and seekers of guidance plainly prepares their weaker minds for the truth to become apparent.
It restrains the disordered movements of thought arising from habitual suggestions and ingrained, objectionable imitations within their receptive and seeking souls.
Instruction and learning therefore require attention to whatever cleanses the receptacle of entrenched inherited convictions and the obstructive, distracting movements they produce.
Here that is the removal of impediments, called emptying or purification.
Equally necessary is attention to the certain premises that prepare the receptacle to receive an effusion: these function as the positive requisite, called adornment.

arabicClauses.text: أقول : هذا إشارة إلى الجواب الثاني من الايرادين المذكورين ،

review.note: Bare self-evidence denial rejected as merely dialectical.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: this points to the answer to the second of the two objections. Since the questioner claims necessary knowledge precisely where the matter is disputed, he could be answered by saying that an appeal to necessity within the point at issue is not admissible under the discipline of inquiry. The proposition ‘Every self-evident matter is undisputed’ converts by contraposition into ‘Whatever is disputed is not self-evident.’ But this would be dialectical disputation, leaving the substance of the difficulty intact.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: this points to the answer to the second of the two objections. Since the questioner claims necessary knowledge precisely where the matter is disputed, he could be answered by saying that an appeal to necessity within the point at issue is not admissible under the discipline of inquiry. The proposition ‘Every self-evident matter is undisputed’ converts by contraposition into ‘Whatever is disputed is not self-evident.’ But this would be dialectical disputation, leaving the substance of the difficulty intact.

arabicClauses.text: فالجواب الحاسم لمادة الشبهة ان يقال ،

review.note: Four alternatives for particular existence are enumerated in order.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: The answer that cuts off its source is to say that a particular possible existence—meaning existence specified by determinations, relations, and relative privative states—cannot be an instance of unrestricted existence in the required sense. For what is meant by the particular existences alleged to be its instances must be one of the following: the subject of those determinations, without considering the accruing determinations along with it; those accruing determinations, without considering their subject at all; or the subject together with the accruing determination. In the last case the determination is considered either as something accruing to the subject or as a constituent part. Four exhaustive alternatives result, both intellectually and in existence. None permits unrestricted existence to have instances that are possible in themselves.

review.note: First (bare subject) versus second (accident alone) distinguished.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Under the first, what is meant is the subject of some determination, attribute, or state without considering that feature along with it. This is in truth pure, one existence, necessary through itself. Under the second, what is meant is an incidentally existing feature without considering the existence which exists through itself along with it. We do not concede that such a feature is an instance of unrestricted existence: under that consideration it is intrinsically nonexistent. How, then, could existent be predicated of it as what it is, making it an instance? An instance of existence is what exists through itself and of which the concept of existence is truly predicated as what it is.

review.note: Fourth (subject under accidental qualification) and intrinsic/relative unity preserved.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Under the fourth alternative, what is meant is the subject of an accruing feature insofar as it is that feature's subject: the feature is considered along with it as accruing to it, as is actually the case externally. Particular existences in external reality are simply that to which these determinations belong. Under this consideration each particular existence is intrinsically identical with the others; indeed, all of them together are nothing but one reality necessary through itself. englishSentences.text: I say: this points to the answer to the second of the two objections.

Since the questioner claims necessary knowledge precisely where the matter is disputed, he could be answered by saying that an appeal to necessity within the point at issue is not admissible under the discipline of inquiry.

The proposition ‘Every self-evident matter is undisputed’ converts by contraposition into ‘Whatever is disputed is not self-evident.’ But this would be dialectical disputation, leaving the substance of the difficulty intact.

The answer that cuts off its source is to say that a particular possible existence—meaning existence specified by determinations, relations, and relative privative states—cannot be an instance of unrestricted existence in the required sense.

For what is meant by the particular existences alleged to be its instances must be one of the following: the subject of those determinations, without considering the accruing determinations along with it;
those accruing determinations, without considering their subject at all;
or the subject together with the accruing determination.
In the last case the determination is considered either as something accruing to the subject or as a constituent part.
Four exhaustive alternatives result, both intellectually and in existence.
None permits unrestricted existence to have instances that are possible in themselves.
Under the first, what is meant is the subject of some determination, attribute, or state without considering that feature along with it.
This is in truth pure, one existence, necessary through itself.
Under the second, what is meant is an incidentally existing feature without considering the existence which exists through itself along with it.
We do not concede that such a feature is an instance of unrestricted existence: under that consideration it is intrinsically nonexistent.
How, then, could existent be predicated of it as what it is, making it an instance?
An instance of existence is what exists through itself and of which the concept of existence is truly predicated as what it is.
Under the third, what is meant is the sum of both, a composite of the accruing feature and its subject.
We do not concede that such a composite can exist, since, as they themselves establish, existence cannot be a constituent of quiddities in external reality.
On this supposition the intellectual instances would therefore be intrinsically impossible in external things.
Differences among the instances of existence would follow, although their impossibility has already been demonstrated.

You may object that the impossible consequence follows only if the composite is impossible without qualification, whereas its being impossible externally alone need not be impossible in the required sense.
I reply that anything which is an instance of unrestricted existence, and of which existence is predicated as what it is, must require existence through itself.
It cannot therefore require nonbeing at any of its levels.

Under the fourth alternative, what is meant is the subject of an accruing feature insofar as it is that feature's subject: the feature is considered along with it as accruing to it, as is actually the case externally.
Particular existences in external reality are simply that to which these determinations belong.
Under this consideration each particular existence is intrinsically identical with the others;
indeed, all of them together are nothing but one reality necessary through itself.
What belongs intrinsically does not change through the addition of concomitants and accruing features.
Unity is intrinsic to it, while multiplicity consists in features accruing through attributes that are intrinsically nonexistent and exist incidentally.
It is therefore only these intrinsically nonexistent concomitants, additional to the essence, that are qualified by possibility.

This investigation establishes that unrestricted existence as unrestricted existence cannot possess intrinsic instances differing in necessity, possibility, and impossibility, because genuine unity belongs to it intrinsically.

It further clarifies what we explained in the prolegomenon: possibility accrues in consideration of the manifest aspect of knowledge, and necessity in consideration of the manifest aspect of existence.
The distinction between their manifest aspects is evident.
As for the assertion that the possible and the necessary exclude each other, it rests upon positing multiple instances of existence and assigning necessity to one rather than the others.
The defect in that position has already been explained, so there is no need to prolong the discussion.

arabicClauses.text: أقول : هذا ايراد بعض على ما برهن عليه ،

review.note: Mental existence objection to equal modal status stated as opponent's.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: this presents a counter-instance to the demonstration that instances of unrestricted existence cannot differ in necessity, possibility, and impossibility. Mental existence is one of the divisions, and therefore one of the instances, of unrestricted existence. Yet, insofar as it is mental, it cannot exist externally: otherwise it would cease to be mental existence. The Necessary is likewise an instance of unrestricted existence, yet must exist externally through itself. Its instances would therefore differ in necessity and impossibility.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: The answer is that mental being is intrinsically the same as external being, though it differs from it in consideration. Establishing this requires a preliminary explanation. Unrestricted existence, in the sense adopted by the people of realization—not the meaning conventionally adopted by later thinkers, as the prolegomenon explained—has primary states. These are called intrinsic affairs because they require the essence to manifest according to them. Or, equivalently, the essence requires that it manifest according to them, coloured by their governing properties, so as to display the perfections of the names necessarily accompanying essential perfection. This will be explained in detail, God willing.

review.note: Names/fixed entities and sequence spirits–imaginal–sensible retained.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Those affairs, called fixed entities at another level and names under another consideration, differ in comprehensiveness and essential proximity. Some are universals whose manifestation actually encompasses the manifestation of all the particulars falling under them; these are called levels. The essence cannot manifest in the more remote levels without first manifesting in the nearer. Manifestation proceeds through these comprehensive levels, from the world of spirits and the imaginal world, until it reaches completion in the world of sense. This is the last of the comprehensive levels, which the people of realization call loci of disclosure. In another terminology, existence at this level is called external being.

englishSentences.text: I say: this presents a counter-instance to the demonstration that instances of unrestricted existence cannot differ in necessity, possibility, and impossibility.
Mental existence is one of the divisions, and therefore one of the instances, of unrestricted existence.
Yet, insofar as it is mental, it cannot exist externally: otherwise it would cease to be mental existence.
The Necessary is likewise an instance of unrestricted existence, yet must exist externally through itself.
Its instances would therefore differ in necessity and impossibility.
It should not be replied that what cannot exist externally is the thing in the mind insofar as it is in the mind, not mental being itself, which belongs among external accidents.
On this reply, mental being means the occurrence of an intelligible form, and that form, insofar as it accrues to intellects, unquestionably exists externally.
For we answer that intelligible forms are what accrue to intellects, whereas what constitutes their being there is something else, distinct from the form itself.
Intellect considers it when attending to the form's coming to be within intellect.
It thus occurs at the second level of intellection, cannot exist externally, and yields the difference just alleged.
The answer is that mental being is intrinsically the same as external being, though it differs from it in consideration.
Establishing this requires a preliminary explanation.
Unrestricted existence, in the sense adopted by the people of realization—not the meaning conventionally adopted by later thinkers, as the prolegomenon explained—has primary states.
These are called intrinsic affairs because they require the essence to manifest according to them.

Or, equivalently, the essence requires that it manifest according to them, coloured by their governing properties, so as to display the perfections of the names necessarily accompanying essential perfection.
This will be explained in detail, God willing.
Those affairs, called fixed entities at another level and names under another consideration, differ in comprehensiveness and essential proximity.
Some are universals whose manifestation actually encompasses the manifestation of all the particulars falling under them;
these are called levels.
The essence cannot manifest in the more remote levels without first manifesting in the nearer.
Manifestation proceeds through these comprehensive levels, from the world of spirits and the imaginal world, until it reaches completion in the world of sense.
This is the last of the comprehensive levels, which the people of realization call loci of disclosure.
In another terminology, existence at this level is called external being.
Now recall what the preceding discussions have established.

These states and the judgments that follow them in specifying existence—whether comprehensive states called levels or particular states encompassed by them—are merely conceptual considerations and privative relations.
They do not enter into the reality of existence as such.
Mental being, which is one of those levels, is therefore intrinsically external being, though distinct in consideration.
Intelligible meanings too accrue to external being, but at certain levels or on condition that it is qualified by other accruing attributes.
Some concomitants arise only after a prior concomitant has attached, as explained above.
In short, all these considerations and judgments, at whatever level, belong only to external being: it is last in manifestation and first in rank.
Take heed.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: after establishing the first objective through reflective investigation and inference, answering the possible objections, and refuting the opponent's position by exposing the weakness of its foundations—as promised at the opening—the author wishes to add an indication to those discussions. It will suffice for the denying opponent who looks with fairness and consideration, while giving the aspiring student further disclosure and insight. Its purpose is to intimate that the objective belongs among self-evident matters which do not need such indications for their acquisition. The point is that they attribute to the Necessary's existent reality and identity something incompatible with the attributes which they themselves hold must belong to Him. Any doctrine or judgment incompatible with His necessary concomitants will reveal its falsity to someone who examines it attentively. Hence the author calls this discussion an indication.

arabicClauses.text: و بيان ذلك ،

review.note: Particular Necessary as wholly unlike its effects is set beside its shared general and existential predicates.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: They believe that the Necessary is a particular specific existent reality: a particular external being intrinsically different from all other external beings. Yet they also hold it to be the principle and cause of all the other beings and species, while asserting separation and the absence of any affinity. At the same time they place it under unrestricted external existence, which encompasses all the external things dependent on it, whatever account they give of existence—whether a conceptual consideration, as some hold, or a reality, as the others maintain. In short, they judge it to fall under existence, just as under the other comprehensive universals and general notions: being a reality, a cause, a determinate thing, and one. They also place it under many further universals, the attributes they hold necessarily established of it, such as being knowing, powerful, willing, and the rest.

review.note: The argument is a purported inconsistency between absolute dissimilarity, causality, priority and shared universals.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: But to attribute principiality—which is itself a relation—and priority to something plainly conflicts with denying every affinity between it and any of its effects. Denying affinity likewise conflicts with holding it to share in external being, which is what its particular existent reality is said to be. Its inclusion under any universal or general notion similarly conflicts with denying affinity between it and all effects, and entails sharing something with the other external species included under that common notion. Anyone who has caught the scent of certainty about existence can see that such an account of the Necessary is far from clear intuition—indeed, from sound intellect and correct thought—because of its manifest contradiction and explicit impossibility.

review.note: Reply rejects genuinely distinct existential instances but retains relational differences.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: We reply that the preceding discussions, together with the experiential indications and rational demonstrations to follow, establish that existence cannot have instances with different realities qua existence, such that unrestricted existence would be predicated of them accidentally and in a graded manner. Anyone even slightly trained in the methods of discerning people with perfected spiritual taste and excellent acquired dispositions will also recognize the necessary judgment that external being, shared by the external beings through which entities come to be outside the mind, must itself be external being. Those beings, whether external or mental, must be the very reality and nature of that being. Their differences and multiplicity arise only through the particularizing relations and conceptually considered correlations. As repeatedly explained, what they understand by the word existence as a mere intellectual consideration has no standing in the vocabulary of realization.

englishSentences.text: I say: after establishing the first objective through reflective investigation and inference, answering the possible objections, and refuting the opponent's position by exposing the weakness of its foundations—as promised at the opening—the author wishes to add an indication to those discussions.
It will suffice for the denying opponent who looks with fairness and consideration, while giving the aspiring student further disclosure and insight.
Its purpose is to intimate that the objective belongs among self-evident matters which do not need such indications for their acquisition.
The point is that they attribute to the Necessary's existent reality and identity something incompatible with the attributes which they themselves hold must belong to Him.
Any doctrine or judgment incompatible with His necessary concomitants will reveal its falsity to someone who examines it attentively.
Hence the author calls this discussion an indication.
They believe that the Necessary is a particular specific existent reality: a particular external being intrinsically different from all other external beings.
Yet they also hold it to be the principle and cause of all the other beings and species, while asserting separation and the absence of any affinity.

At the same time they place it under unrestricted external existence, which encompasses all the external things dependent on it, whatever account they give of existence—whether a conceptual consideration, as some hold, or a reality, as the others maintain.
In short, they judge it to fall under existence, just as under the other comprehensive universals and general notions: being a reality, a cause, a determinate thing, and one.
They also place it under many further universals, the attributes they hold necessarily established of it, such as being knowing, powerful, willing, and the rest.
But to attribute principiality—which is itself a relation—and priority to something plainly conflicts with denying every affinity between it and any of its effects.
Denying affinity likewise conflicts with holding it to share in external being, which is what its particular existent reality is said to be.

Its inclusion under any universal or general notion similarly conflicts with denying affinity between it and all effects, and entails sharing something with the other external species included under that common notion.

Anyone who has caught the scent of certainty about existence can see that such an account of the Necessary is far from clear intuition—indeed, from sound intellect and correct thought—because of its manifest contradiction and explicit impossibility.
An objection may be raised that the commonality required in these cases concerns only extrinsic accruing predicates.
On their view unrestricted being accrues to the necessary existent reality;
principiality too is one of the privative relations and extrinsic concomitants arising when it is considered in relation to external things.
The same applies to other comprehensive universals, such as quiddity and causality.
Moreover, on their account existence is an intellectual consideration which accrues mentally to existent realities and particular existences, as are the other comprehensive attributes.
Their necessary reality and the dependent existent realities can therefore share such considerations without contradicting their extramental separation.

We reply that the preceding discussions, together with the experiential indications and rational demonstrations to follow, establish that existence cannot have instances with different realities qua existence, such that unrestricted existence would be predicated of them accidentally and in a graded manner.

Anyone even slightly trained in the methods of discerning people with perfected spiritual taste and excellent acquired dispositions will also recognize the necessary judgment that external being, shared by the external beings through which entities come to be outside the mind, must itself be external being.
Those beings, whether external or mental, must be the very reality and nature of that being.
Their differences and multiplicity arise only through the particularizing relations and conceptually considered correlations.
As repeatedly explained, what they understand by the word existence as a mere intellectual consideration has no standing in the vocabulary of realization.
The author's concluding injunction to reflect points toward answering these two objections.

review.note: Author's irony/rhetorical purpose preserved despite source's uncertain التغيير reading.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: We reply that, after refuting the opponent's claim that determinations and quiddities are external realities rather than that through which they come to be, this expression is preferable to others for its irony and reproach. These can impel the opponent to abandon his conviction—indeed, sever those deeply rooted beliefs from his inward being—in accordance with the art of rhetoric. Determinate things, precisely as determinate, must therefore be regarded as intellectual meanings and natures taken with conceptually considered relations and correlations. This reverses the view that unrestricted being is merely a consideration occurring at the second level of intellection, while the intrinsically real things are determinate quiddities.

arabicClauses.text: و هذا في النظائر المحسوسة ،

review.note: Light/color analogy preserves partial perceptual report and source's difficult ophthalmic metaphor.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: In sensible experience this resembles someone whose weak sight leads him to suppose that the different colours alone manifest themselves to perception externally, and that unrestricted light, which is evident in itself and makes other things evident, has no external manifestation except within colours. Such a judgment arises from the accumulated obscuration of compound ignorance, produced by ingrained uncritical adherence, which prevents perception of light apart from dense, dark loci of manifestation. A discerning knower need not contradict what such people report, but should acknowledge the condition they are actually describing: their report concerns the limit of their apprehension and the point at which their visual ray comes to rest. Because of its weakness it does not go beyond colours.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: In sensible experience this resembles someone whose weak sight leads him to suppose that the different colours alone manifest themselves to perception externally, and that unrestricted light, which is evident in itself and makes other things evident, has no external manifestation except within colours. Such a judgment arises from the accumulated obscuration of compound ignorance, produced by ingrained uncritical adherence, which prevents perception of light apart from dense, dark loci of manifestation. A discerning knower need not contradict what such people report, but should acknowledge the condition they are actually describing: their report concerns the limit of their apprehension and the point at which their visual ray comes to rest. Because of its weakness it does not go beyond colours.

englishSentences.text: I say: the author has established the question as intended and rejected positions liable to mislead the discerning student, exposing where their adherents stumble.

He has removed the powerful doubts and evident difficulties that led them into error—difficulties escaped only by sound intellects and upright minds after refinement of the inward secret and precision of reflection, aided by clear intuition and a share of spiritual taste and certainty.

He now wishes to explain genuine undifferentiated comprehensiveness and intrinsic unrestrictedness, so that the way in which the differentiated names arise from it may be established upon this foundation.
This completes his purpose and fulfils his undertaking to explain divine unity according to the vocabulary of realization.
Such an account must bring distinction and gathering together, and transcend both the exclusive assertion of incomparability and assimilation.
That is what the reality of divine unity requires, as the saying attributed here to al-Ṣādiq, peace be upon him, indicates: ‘Gathering without distinction is heresy;
distinction without gathering is divestment;

joining the two is divine unity.’

The author therefore says that it is more fitting and more necessary to identify real external being with unrestricted being which encompasses all determinations.
The explanation is that external being, as established above, subsists through itself and sustains the determinate quiddities conjoined with it.
Insofar as they are determinate, those quiddities are intellectual meanings and natures taken together with conceptually considered relations and correlations.
They have no existence except in relation to external being.
It is therefore undoubtedly more fitting to identify unrestricted necessary being with external being than with those determinations.
It should not be objected that the language of ‘more fitting’ is inappropriate because it signifies merely the preference of one alternative over another, whereas that is not the intended conclusion.

We reply that, after refuting the opponent's claim that determinations and quiddities are external realities rather than that through which they come to be, this expression is preferable to others for its irony and reproach.
These can impel the opponent to abandon his conviction—indeed, sever those deeply rooted beliefs from his inward being—in accordance with the art of rhetoric.
Determinate things, precisely as determinate, must therefore be regarded as intellectual meanings and natures taken with conceptually considered relations and correlations.
This reverses the view that unrestricted being is merely a consideration occurring at the second level of intellection, while the intrinsically real things are determinate quiddities.

In sensible experience this resembles someone whose weak sight leads him to suppose that the different colours alone manifest themselves to perception externally, and that unrestricted light, which is evident in itself and makes other things evident, has no external manifestation except within colours.

Such a judgment arises from the accumulated obscuration of compound ignorance, produced by ingrained uncritical adherence, which prevents perception of light apart from dense, dark loci of manifestation.

A discerning knower need not contradict what such people report, but should acknowledge the condition they are actually describing: their report concerns the limit of their apprehension and the point at which their visual ray comes to rest.
Because of its weakness it does not go beyond colours.

‘When a person has no sound eye,
it is no wonder that he doubts, though morning shines.’

This too is a level of the Real's manifestation according to their faculties of awareness, a locus of His perfection and a place of His beauty's disclosure, and so is not to be denied.
Hence the author and other people of realization do not simply judge their position and other positions to be false.
This meaning too may be sensed in his expression ‘more fitting’.
‘All within Your sanctuary love You;

yet
I alone [am] for all within Your sanctuary.’

arabicClauses.text: أقول : متى تقرَّر ان الكون الحقيقي العيني القائم بنفسه القيُّوم لغيره ،

review.note: Genuine unity and the notion of the first designation are attributed to Ibn Turka.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: once it is established that real external being, self-subsistent and sustaining others, is unrestricted being, it is unquestionably genuinely one. The other quiddities and particularities, considered precisely as such, are nonentities. Anyone who has purified his heart of natural impurities and freed his soul and faculties from inherited convictions and imaginative and estimative forms can then see that the Real, glorified is He, is unrestricted existence without difference or multiplicity. Genuine intrinsic unity is what He requires through Himself, and is the first name and first expression by which He is designated.

review.note: Multiplicity belongs to levels and names, not to unrestricted identity itself.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Multiplicity and difference are intelligible only where duality and plurality can be conceived and where some part has a judgment not belonging to another. How could the genuinely one, unrestricted reality encompassing the many—everything outside which is sheer negation and nonbeing—be subject to difference and multiplicity? Difference and multiplicity may indeed be conceived in the levels of its descent and loci of its manifestation according to its intrinsic affairs and states, where the relations of the names encounter one another and the conceptual correlations differ.

arabicClauses.text: و امّا حضرة الإطلاق الذاتي المعبَّر عنه عند القوم بغيب الهويَّة و اللاتعيُّن فلا مجال للاعتبارات فيه أصلًا ،

review.note: No real name or definition applies in the unqualified register; the terms are explained through conceptual consideration.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: But in the presence of intrinsic unrestrictedness, which the people of this discipline call the hiddenness of identity and nondetermination, no considerations have any place—not even this consideration. No conceptually considered concomitant mingles with it. It is sheer, pure existence, unmixed with anything else. In this respect, namely intrinsic unrestrictedness, it has neither composition nor multiplicity; indeed, it has neither any real name nor a descriptive definition. In their terminology a name is the essence considered under some meaning, whether privative or existential; they call that meaning an attribute or qualification. Where there is no attribute there is no name, and where nothing is considered along with the essence there is no attribute. Under this consideration the essence is unrestricted, with no determinations or particularizing aspects taken into account, and is therefore stripped of all judgments and names.

arabicClauses.text: و اما قوله : « و سلب ما عدا الإطلاق عنه » فهو جواب دخل مقدَّر ،

review.note: The apparent self-reference reductio and response by negative/non-real determination are distinguished.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: The author's words, ‘Negating everything other than unrestrictedness of it,’ answer an implicit objection. The rule that attributing meanings and judgments to the essence requires considering their origins in relations and determinations appears to be refuted by this very judgment. Negating everything other than unrestrictedness is itself a judgment, yet it presupposes none of those features; otherwise the supposition would be contradicted. He answers that, although this is a judgment, it is negative, so its source is a determination that is not real in the relevant sense. The discussion concerns real determinations and real names; this is therefore not a valid counter-objection. ‘Counter-objection’ here means a general rebuttal, although the word is more commonly used for a detailed rebuttal of a particular premise. The former sense is more evident here.

arabicClauses.text: فان قلت : التعيُّنات مطلقا على ما ذهبتم إليه لا يكون اموراً حقيقيَّة بل اعتباريَّة عدميَّة سواء كان مبدأ للاحكام الوجوديَّة أو السلبيَّة فلا وجه حينئذ للتخصيص .

review.note: Difference between non-real and real name-producing considerations retained without making determinations new substances.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: You may object that, on this account, all determinations are conceptually considered, privative matters rather than realities, whether they ground existential or negative judgments. There is therefore no reason for the distinction. I reply that, although all determinations are matters of consideration, there is a difference between those that can ground real names and those that cannot. When intellect considers another meaning along with the essence, whether existential or privative, a real name arises for the essence under that meaning. But when it considers the essence stripped of all meanings and judgments, even of this consideration itself, no determination or particular form arises capable of serving as such a ground. When the soul nevertheless conceives it, that conception acquires an incidental determination from the particular features of the receptacle in which it occurs. Without intellect's consideration, the reality itself would not require this determination. This is the non-real determination grounding the negative judgments now under discussion. It is this consideration that licenses the expressions nondetermination, unrestricted existence, and hiddenness of identity.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: It should not be objected that it therefore no longer remains purely unrestricted once this consideration is added. Intellect can abstract from the consideration even while it accrues, since intellect can abstract things from the very descriptions under which it conceives them—as with the wholly unknown, the wholly nonexistent, and other unrestricted concepts discussed earlier. Take heed. Then reflect on the expressions ‘gathering-place of opposites’ and ‘the presence where opposites press together’, and on the subtle question in which unaided intellect has no scope. Do so with refined certainty and a purified orientation, so that the Real may become apparent according to your degree. The author's ‘reflect’ points to subtleties of this kind.

englishSentences.text: I say: once it is established that real external being, self-subsistent and sustaining others, is unrestricted being, it is unquestionably genuinely one.
The other quiddities and particularities, considered precisely as such, are nonentities.

Anyone who has purified his heart of natural impurities and freed his soul and faculties from inherited convictions and imaginative and estimative forms can then see that the Real, glorified is He, is unrestricted existence without difference or multiplicity.
Genuine intrinsic unity is what He requires through Himself, and is the first name and first expression by which He is designated.
Multiplicity and difference are intelligible only where duality and plurality can be conceived and where some part has a judgment not belonging to another.
How could the genuinely one, unrestricted reality encompassing the many—everything outside which is sheer negation and nonbeing—be subject to difference and multiplicity?

Difference and multiplicity may indeed be conceived in the levels of its descent and loci of its manifestation according to its intrinsic affairs and states, where the relations of the names encounter one another and the conceptual correlations differ.

But in the presence of intrinsic unrestrictedness, which the people of this discipline call the hiddenness of identity and nondetermination, no considerations have any place—not even this consideration.
No conceptually considered concomitant mingles with it.
It is sheer, pure existence, unmixed with anything else.
In this respect, namely intrinsic unrestrictedness, it has neither composition nor multiplicity;
indeed, it has neither any real name nor a descriptive definition.
In their terminology a name is the essence considered under some meaning, whether privative or existential;
they call that meaning an attribute or qualification.
Where there is no attribute there is no name, and where nothing is considered along with the essence there is no attribute.
Under this consideration the essence is unrestricted, with no determinations or particularizing aspects taken into account, and is therefore stripped of all judgments and names.
Nevertheless, when this very consideration is entertained, a name does arise for the essence through it.
It is not, however, one of the real names: it arises not from considering a meaning together with the essence but from not considering meanings.
The objection that this is itself a meaning does not overturn the principle.
It is not one of the real meanings, since its nature is precisely to negate and remove the consideration of a meaning.
Its possessing the status of a meaning thus arises only by supposition and consideration.
Hence the author qualifies ‘names’ with ‘real’.

It is also clear that no descriptive definition is available: such a definition proceeds through properties, which are attributes peculiar to a thing, and negating the general class excludes its particular members.
The author's words, ‘Negating everything other than unrestrictedness of it,’ answer an implicit objection.
The rule that attributing meanings and judgments to the essence requires considering their origins in relations and determinations appears to be refuted by this very judgment.
Negating everything other than unrestrictedness is itself a judgment, yet it presupposes none of those features;
otherwise the supposition would be contradicted.
He answers that, although this is a judgment, it is negative, so its source is a determination that is not real in the relevant sense.
The discussion concerns real determinations and real names;
this is therefore not a valid counter-objection.
‘Counter-objection’ here means a general rebuttal, although the word is more commonly used for a detailed rebuttal of a particular premise.
The former sense is more evident here.
You may object that, on this account, all determinations are conceptually considered, privative matters rather than realities, whether they ground existential or negative judgments.
There is therefore no reason for the distinction.
I reply that, although all determinations are matters of consideration, there is a difference between those that can ground real names and those that cannot.
When intellect considers another meaning along with the essence, whether existential or privative, a real name arises for the essence under that meaning.
But when it considers the essence stripped of all meanings and judgments, even of this consideration itself, no determination or particular form arises capable of serving as such a ground.
When the soul nevertheless conceives it, that conception acquires an incidental determination from the particular features of the receptacle in which it occurs.
Without intellect's consideration, the reality itself would not require this determination.
This is the non-real determination grounding the negative judgments now under discussion.
It is this consideration that licenses the expressions nondetermination, unrestricted existence, and hiddenness of identity.
It should not be objected that it therefore no longer remains purely unrestricted once this consideration is added.

Intellect can abstract from the consideration even while it accrues, since intellect can abstract things from the very descriptions under which it conceives them—as with the wholly unknown, the wholly nonexistent, and other unrestricted concepts discussed earlier.
Take heed.
Then reflect on the expressions ‘gathering-place of opposites’ and ‘the presence where opposites press together’, and on the subtle question in which unaided intellect has no scope.
Do so with refined certainty and a purified orientation, so that the Real may become apparent according to your degree.
The author's ‘reflect’ points to subtleties of this kind.

arabicClauses.text: أقول : هذا شروع في بيان تفريع التفصيل الاسمائى على الإجمال الذاتي و كيفية انتشاء تلك الأسماء باجناسها و أنواعها و أصنافها و تعيين متعلّقات كل منها و مواطن اعتبارها فان لكل اسم مبدأ لا يظهر ذلك الا في موطن خاص من مواطن تنوعات الذات و مرتبة مخصوصة من مراتب تنزلاتها لا يطلق ذلك الاسم عليها الا بذلك الاعتبار و هذا معنى من معانى ما عليه ائمّة الشريعة رضى اللَّه عنهم انّ - أسماء الحق توقيفيّة و ذلك من امهات - أبواب - مسائل هذا الفنّ كما سبق - بيانه في المقدمة ،

review.note: Opening differentiates names by proper domain and levels; tawqīfī now retained as authoritatively fixed, not a distinct act of disclosure. Technical vocabulary used as controlled correspondence with reflective investigators.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: I say: this begins the explanation of how the differentiation of the names branches from essential undifferentiated comprehensiveness, how those names arise in their genera, species, and kinds, and what each concerns and where it is considered. Every name has a source which appears only in a particular domain of the essence's varieties and at a particular level of its descent. The name is applied to the essence only under that consideration. This is one sense of the authorities of the revealed law's statement that the Real's names are tawqīfī—authoritatively fixed. It is among the fundamental questions of this discipline, as the prolegomenon explained. As has repeatedly been said, this treatise addresses reflective investigators and reasoners according to their established ways of presenting arguments and demonstrations. We must therefore not depart from their familiar technical terms and customary forms of address. We descend to the range of their understanding, in the hope that God may release them from the confinement of their estimations. At the same time, instruction requires us to draw attention to the terms used by the people of this discipline and to interpret the author's words through their terminology, making matters easier for students seeking guidance. A subtle affinity joins the experiential meanings disclosed through unveiling to the terms that express them in this vocabulary. That affinity greatly assists understanding, yet is discerned only through the light of sainthood and the niche of prophecy. We should therefore explain something of it in the course of these lines.

arabicClauses.text: إذا عرفت هذا فاعلم ان الذات باعتبار اللاتعيُّن المسمّاة بغيب الغيب ،

review.note: One intrinsic unrestricted unity distinguished from relational numerical unity; the electronic Arabic duplicates one unit about unrestricted identity and the whole—not a different doctrinal proposition.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Know that the essence considered under nondetermination, called now the unseen of the unseen and now absolute identity, cannot include any consideration entailing determination, restriction, multiplicity, or plurality. The first descriptive meaning considered of it is genuine unity, in which neither multiplicity nor otherness can be considered in any respect. Multiplicity itself does not differ from unity relative to it, just as unity does not differ from the essence. This is clarified by the earlier distinction between two senses of unity. The first is absolute intrinsic unity, whose concept includes nothing suggesting a multiplicity of aspects or duality. Even the non-consideration of multiplicity is not included, since it would suggest opposition to multiplicity and thereby entail duality. The second is relational unity: a thing's not being divided into participating items insofar as it is considered in that way. This is the unity opposed to multiplicity, whether accidentally or intrinsically. Here unity is understood in the first sense, and absolute identity denotes that which is one through it. Under this consideration the essence has universal comprehensiveness from which no level is excluded, even sensible things. Consequently, the relation of knowledge necessarily belongs to it through its being present to itself in itself.

arabicClauses.text:
ثمَّ انّ هاهنا مقدمة اخرى لا بدّ من الوقوف عليها و هي ان الظهور

المذكور لمّا كان مستلزماً للشعور بسائر الشئون و الأحوال و الاعتبارات للذات بمراتبها و أحوالها و أحكامها و لوازمها كلّها حتى المحسوسات على وجه كلي جملى ،

review.note: Essential perfection and perfection of the names are distinct by reference to hiddenness and manifestation, not two separate divine essences.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Another preliminary distinction must be understood. The manifestation just described entails awareness of all the essence's affairs, states, and considerations, with their levels, conditions, governing properties, and necessary concomitants, including sensible things, in a universal and comprehensive manner. The object of that awareness may be the essence in its hiddenness, with everything established and witnessed within it, as all numerical levels are established in one. In their terminology this awareness is called essential perfection. It entails absolute self-sufficiency: the essence manifests in its hiddenness to itself in the manner described, without needing to assume alien forms or pass through the cycles of otherness. Alternatively, the object may be the intrinsic affairs themselves, through the manifestation of their entities to themselves or of some to others within the levels. In that case this awareness is called the perfection of the names.

review.note: Existence and knowledge differ relationally in their objects at the manifest side, not by a separated essential subject.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: Under the first consideration there is no otherness between the essence and any of the four names, or between one of those names and another. Considered from the side of manifestation, existence concerns the affairs just mentioned insofar as they manifest; knowledge concerns them too, but insofar as they are objects of knowledge in the world of meanings. Their manifest aspects are thus relationally distinguished in this presence of comprehensive unity.

‘Cognition is not constituted merely by presence to an immaterial thing, nor by any arbitrary kind of presence falling under the unrestricted term, as already explained. What is required is the presence of a thing to an immaterial being that exerts some kind of influence upon it. If that being intrinsically necessitates the thing cognized, without depending on another for this necessitation, its cognition requires no additional condition beyond that necessitation. Otherwise—if it does not necessitate it—another condition is needed: conjunction with it in the manner of an accident's conjunction with its subject, securing the influence required. This does not contradict our account of necessitation. Necessitation makes the effect related and close to its necessitating principle as the principle is related to itself. Requiring the weaker does not exclude the stronger.’ Here ends his statement.

arabicClauses.englishCorrespondence: An alert reader will recognize its substance: the reality of cognition—intellectual cognition ascribed to immaterial beings—is not presence without qualification, but a particular presence consisting in an agent's having present its effect connected with it. This varies with the cognizing agents' efficacy. The stronger the agent's influence and the less it needs intermediaries, the stronger that connection; the weaker its influence and the more intermediaries it requires, the weaker the connection. Some agents attain the strength of intrinsic necessitation, producing an effect so that its connection with the agent is like the agent's connection with itself, without any intermediaries or instruments. This is the utmost efficacy, beyond which nothing more can be conceived. The relational connection and subtle unifying link with the cognized object likewise admit no increase. Others are so weak that they cannot act without an additional will and choice and, even then, need many intermediaries and diverse causes. This is the extremity of weakness in efficacy; the relational connection and subtle unifying link are correspondingly weak and remote, eventually reaching merely accidental conjunction [a contextual reading of the displayed alternatives].
